extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, practicing reporters, media critics, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for ethical journalism practice, including avoiding fabrication/plagiarism, calling falsehoods what they are, verifying claims, and understanding journalism's role as a check on power. Emphasizes how reporters should adjust coverage when confronted with deliberate lies versus gaffes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cutting corners / ethical slippery slopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Slippery slopes people can find themselves on when they start to cut corners, especially when they are struggling with personal challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and warn students and reporters about the small compromises that lead to larger ethical failings; use talks, mentoring, and concrete examples (e.g., predecessors who fabricated) to highlight how minor shortcuts can escalate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and counter cognitive dissonance / self-justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often employ cognitive dissonance—the idea that they are good people so they will never do something like what I did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about ethical self-justification; explicitly address personal vulnerabilities and pressures that can lead to lapses in judgment; incorporate ethical reflection into newsroom training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism, fabrication, and bias are core ethical failings in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict standards against copying others' work, inventing facts, and allowing unexamined bias to shape reporting; enforce editorial checks to prevent these violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call a lie a lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Not calling a lie a lie is [one of] the biggest ethical failings in media today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply reproduce false statements verbatim without labeling them; editors and reporters should exercise judgment to explicitly identify falsehoods rather than treating all statements as neutral 'quotes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify, fact-check, and corroborate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When public figures make factual claims (e.g., '81 percent of white homicide victims are killed by blacks' or 'thousands of New Jersey Muslims celebrating 9/11'), the truth can be drowned out if claims are not checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate context and authoritative statistics (citations such as FBI data), seek corroboration for claims, and make clear when evidence is lacking; use real-time fact-checking where appropriate rather than mere repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between gaffes and deliberate lies; adapt coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: We have shifted from covering political gaffes to covering lies. That adjustment is proving to be difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change editorial practices to treat deliberate falsehoods differently than accidental mistakes—prioritize verification, context, and explicit labeling; rethink beat and campaign coverage habits that default to neutral quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold journalism's public-service mission and accountability role
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism serves as a check on the absolute power of government, 'comforts the afflicted and afflicts the comfortable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the democratic and watchdog functions of journalism guide reporting choices; emphasize accountability, public-interest reporting, and courage to challenge powerful figures rather than merely amplifying them.
